records.title: Alqueva: water allocation, pumping energy and staged expansion
aliases: Empreendimento de Fins Múltiplos de Alqueva
records.answer: Alqueva is a regional water system whose irrigation, public-supply and energy functions depend on each other. Its recent decisions are most useful when water allowances, prices, pumping infrastructure and solar procurement are followed as separate operating questions.
records.scope: One Empreendimento de Fins Múltiplos de Alqueva managed by EDIA, including its connected water-distribution system and component expansion decisions. Individual reservoirs, irrigation blocks, pumping groups and self-consumption plants are not additional counted projects. Separately promoted solar schemes sharing the Alqueva name are not automatically part of these delivery claims.
records.stage: Operating water-system context and dated government allocation, pricing and component-investment accounts inspected. Announced ceilings, procurement and expenditure authorization are not blanket acceptance of every expansion or measured environmental outcomes.

identity_decision.rationale: The government identifies EFMA as one EDIA-managed scheme with connected water uses and infrastructure. This account follows that system rather than counting each irrigation block, pumping group or solar unit. Shared reservoir names do not merge separately promoted investments. No historical acquisition docket is reused.

timeline.event: Government announces procurement for four pumping-station self-consumption solar units.
Government authorizes Vidigueira phase-two and Álamos pumping expenditure, separately describing Cuba-Este as operating.
Government reports national-interest recognition of the hydro-agricultural scheme.
Government announces a conditional revised annual water-use framework and governance requirements.
Government explains contracted-water pricing and separate additional-volume tiers.

sections.heading: A regional system rather than a single dam
sections.text: Alqueva’s identity extends beyond its best-known reservoir. The February 2025 government account places the EDIA-managed scheme within the management of Guadiana and Sado water resources and describes its hydro-agricultural reach across several municipalities. That geography is a service and infrastructure system, not a new city boundary. Irrigation blocks, pumping stations and water-transfer links therefore belong within one connected project account. National-interest recognition describes a public decision about the scheme; it does not certify the condition of every asset. Regional development remains a purpose to assess through evidence, rather than an economic result established by the designation alone.

sections.heading: More allowable water remains conditional
sections.text: The January 16, 2026 announcement raises the stated annual maximum from 620 to 730 cubic hectometres, allocating 690 to irrigation and 40 to public and industrial supply. These are announced ceilings, not volumes actually delivered. Their use remains subject to hydrological conditions, drought contingency arrangements and a permanent 120-cubic-hectometre urban reserve. The same account calls for weekly storage and transfer reporting and revisions to operating contracts. The important connection is between allocation and governance: increasing a maximum does not eliminate scarcity or the need to protect downstream conditions. Actual delivery and reserve records would show how that framework operates.

sections.heading: Contracted and additional water have different incentives
sections.text: The February 13 government explanation preserves the price for contracted volumes while describing tiered charges for water used beyond them. It also raises the stated crop-use limit from 110% to 125% and removes the introductory reduced tariff associated with the scheme’s early years. Those distinctions matter to any account of affordability: an unchanged contracted-water price is not a promise that every user’s total bill stays unchanged. The notice explains an incentive structure rather than supplying a customer quotation. Evaluating its effect requires actual consumption bands, applicable charges and service costs, without treating greater flexibility as guaranteed water availability.

sections.heading: Pumping links water distribution to electricity demand
sections.text: The December 2023 procurement account describes four solar self-consumption units intended to supply dedicated pumping stations. It gives a proposed combined capacity of 52 MWp and estimated production of 90 GWh a year. These figures describe the procurement design, not accepted capacity or measured generation. The connection is important because electricity is a variable cost of moving water through the system. Local generation may change that cost, but the result depends on production, pumping schedules and remaining grid purchases. Other existing plants and separately promoted projects at Alqueva must not be combined into this four-unit delivery claim.

sections.heading: An expansion programme contains several delivery stages
sections.text: The March 2024 account authorizes more than €13.7 million for Vidigueira’s second phase and more than €16 million for Álamos pumping groups three and four. It links the latter to reaching the station’s originally envisaged pumping provision. In the same statement, Cuba-Este’s first-phase floating solar plant is explicitly described as operating. That difference is valuable: one component’s operating status does not establish that the newly funded works are complete. The next account should follow the named circuit and pumping groups through construction, testing and service introduction, then relate their actual water and electricity use to the wider system.

sections.heading: Editorial test for a durable water and energy balance
sections.text: Follow the same operating periods across water stored, water delivered, pumping electricity, reserve levels and downstream obligations. Keep allocations separate from withdrawals and distinguish plant capacity from energy generated. At the farm or municipal connection, assess service availability and cost with the relevant contract category intact. Regional economic claims need their own methods and comparison, rather than being inferred from hectares connected. This would make the relationship between drought resilience, affordability and energy use visible while leaving room for trade-offs. A transparent system account should show constraints and unresolved components alongside the benefits of infrastructure already in use.

next_artifacts: Dated storage, transfer, delivery and reserve records, plus the actual revised operating instruments.
Accepted commissioning and operating data for the four solar units, Vidigueira phase two and Álamos groups three/four.
Comparable water-service, energy-cost and downstream environmental records with explicit periods and denominators.

records.title: Lisbon: drainage, parish services and climate adaptation
records.answer: Lisbon’s service account connects large drainage works with parish-level maintenance, digital renewal and heat-adaptation programmes. The useful distinction is between a design or funding decision and the service residents can actually use.
records.scope: Município de Lisboa, counted as one place across its twenty-four freguesias. Excludes the wider Lisbon metropolitan area and surrounding municipalities. Parish-level programmes and individual drainage structures are components of the city account, not additional place identities.
records.stage: Municipal identity, drainage design and chronology, delegation decisions and ongoing programme descriptions inspected. Excavation milestones, approved funding and future commitments do not establish full-system commissioning or measured city-wide outcomes.

identity_decision.rationale: The municipal account defines twenty-four parishes within Lisbon and explains their delegated responsibilities. This profile retains one municipal identity while distinguishing parish implementation and metropolitan dependencies. Individual parishes, tunnels and programmes are not counted as extra places, and no historical acquisition docket is reused.

timeline.event: Municipal page identifies the administrative reorganization that established the twenty-four-parish map.
Drainage chronology labels Monsanto–Santa Apolónia excavation completion in July, separate from the later content-entry timestamp.
Executive announces renewed parish responsibilities and funding proposals.
Updated article records assembly approval of the July delegation contracts.
Executive announces separate maintenance and digital investments, with its cooperation contracts still subject to assembly approval.
City describes ongoing heat, mobility and reuse programmes at Cidade do Zero.

sections.heading: One municipality with distributed local responsibilities
sections.text: Lisbon’s municipal page identifies twenty-four freguesias, or parishes, following the 2012 administrative reorganization. The city and parish bodies share implementation through delegated responsibilities rather than functioning as interchangeable providers. This account counts the municipality once and keeps the wider metropolitan area outside that identity. The page’s discussion of the 2021–2025 delegation cycle remains historical context; later decisions need their own dates and scope. For a resident, the distinction matters when a pavement, green space or waste problem requires action. A city-level policy can depend on parish execution without every local service having the same budget or delivery stage.

sections.heading: Drainage works combine flood routing and water reuse
sections.text: The drainage plan moves excess runoff between catchments through the Monsanto–Santa Apolónia and Chelas–Beato tunnels. It also describes first-flush storage and treatment, with separate recycled-water pipes for non-potable uses. The chronology labels the first tunnel’s excavation completion in July 2025; that is not full-system commissioning. The tunnel page still presents November 2026 as an estimated excavation endpoint for Chelas–Beato, not a completion receipt. These structures connect underground engineering with conditions at street level and the receiving Tagus. Their effect needs operating evidence across rainfall events, including the performance of capture points, pollution-control basins and the surrounding drainage network.

sections.heading: Delegation approval does not finish parish works
sections.text: The July 29, 2026 article describes renewed responsibilities for cleaning, green-space maintenance and completing previously contracted works. Its September 8 update explicitly records assembly approval of those contracts. The same account says monitoring through November 2025 found works still underway in twenty-three parishes and extends the relevant arrangements through the end of 2027. Approval and the extension therefore support continued implementation rather than prove that the backlog disappeared. The useful follow-up is local: identify the intervention, responsible body, promised completion and actual handover. A total funding announcement cannot show whether each neighbourhood received the intended maintenance or improvement.

sections.heading: Street maintenance and digital renewal need separate measures
sections.text: On September 9, the executive announced roughly €6.5 million for pedestrian surfaces and street furniture, alongside €15 million for digital renewal over three years. Its separate parish-cleaning cooperation contracts were still subject to assembly approval in that account; the previous day’s approval concerned different contracts. These investments address different service problems. Pavement condition and usable furniture require physical observations, while administrative modernization concerns the reliability and accessibility of information and processes. Neither should be measured only by money approved. The proposed digital systems are not already verified improvements in application completion, response time or ease of access for residents.

sections.heading: Climate adaptation reaches schools and ordinary streets
sections.text: The September Cidade do Zero account describes ongoing work on climate refuges, school shade, vegetation and permeable ground, alongside a developing treated-water reuse network. It places these measures beside transport electrification and changes to public space. Their shared practical concern is how people move through and use the city during heat and other stresses. The account also announces a public climate-monitoring platform, not a tested service or a measured reduction in emissions. School and street interventions need location-specific evidence: what was installed, who can reach it and how conditions changed during comparable weather, rather than programme descriptions alone.

sections.heading: Editorial test for resilient everyday services
sections.text: Use selected streets, schools and parish destinations to connect the large infrastructure programme with local maintenance. Record drainage and heat-related conditions over defined weather events, while keeping construction stages separate from commissioned systems. Follow approved contracts to completed interventions and show which body owns the next action. Digital access deserves its own assessment, including whether residents can complete a task without unnecessary repetition or exclusion. This would create a city account that explains both investment and experienced service. It should preserve distinct metropolitan and municipal boundaries and avoid reducing a complex set of local improvements to one unsupported resilience score.

next_artifacts: Commissioning and observed rainfall-event performance for named drainage structures, separate from excavation estimates.
Dated parish contract and work-completion records, preserving the July/September approval sequence.
Location-level climate-adaptation and accessible-service results, plus actual digital delivery and task-completion evidence.

records.title: Porto: urban water, permeable streets and household energy support
records.answer: Porto’s local system links utility management with restored streams, street drainage and advice on household energy improvements. Those services operate at different scales, so their reported capacities and results need to keep their own boundaries.
records.scope: Concelho do Porto, counted as one municipality across seven parish-level units, including three unions of parishes. Excludes the wider metropolitan area, Vila Nova de Gaia and the northern-region reach of Porto Energy Hub. Former parishes and local interventions add no separate place identities.
records.stage: Municipal identity, installed drainage descriptions, utility-reported figures and an energy-advice service inspected. Design capacities, recognition and programme aims are not blanket city-wide performance acceptance.

identity_decision.rationale: The municipality identifies seven parish-level units, including three unions created in the 2013 reorganization. This account follows that municipal boundary while describing regional advice and catchment dependencies separately. Neither former parishes nor the wider Energy Hub territory creates extra Porto places. No historical acquisition docket is reused.

timeline.event: Asprela retrospective identifies the first pilot stream-restoration phase.
Municipal page dates the reorganization producing the current seven parish-level units.
Asprela account dates the Quinta das Lamas daylighting phase.
Asprela account dates the park phase and its three retention basins.
Municipal rain-garden record dates the Rua Santos Pousada intervention, without an exact day.
Municipal climate account publishes utility-reported indicators; the recognition event was October 8.

sections.heading: The municipal boundary is smaller than the service region
sections.text: Porto’s municipal page describes seven parish-level units: four parishes and three unions formed through the 2013 administrative reorganization. This profile counts the municipality once rather than treating constituent or former parishes as separate cities. It also excludes the wider metropolitan area and neighbouring Vila Nova de Gaia. That distinction becomes important when a programme carrying Porto’s name serves a larger territory. The Energy Hub’s northern-region reach, for example, is a service geography rather than a change to the city boundary. Comparisons of local coverage need a matching population or service area instead of borrowing a wider regional denominator.

sections.heading: Utility figures retain their own operating scope
sections.text: The October 27, 2026 municipal account reports non-revenue water falling from 18.6% in 2016 to 11.8% in 2025. It separately reports that 94.8% of the utility’s 2025 energy consumption came from renewable sources and describes up to 1,000 cubic metres a day of non-potable reuse at Freixo. These are different indicators: company energy consumption is not city-wide renewable generation, and an upper reuse figure is not a measured daily delivery series. The account’s international recognition does not replace the underlying operating records. Those records would support a fuller comparison of network efficiency, reuse and continuity of service.

sections.heading: Asprela connects stream restoration with public space
sections.text: The municipal Asprela account traces restoration through a 2009 pilot, a 2015 daylighting phase and the 2022 park intervention. It describes three retention basins with capacity exceeding ten thousand cubic metres, alongside restored stream sections, trees and pedestrian or cycling routes. This combines water management with the ordinary use of a public landscape. The capacity describes what the basins are designed to accommodate, not a measured history of floods avoided. Assessing durability would require maintenance and storm-event evidence, including how the restored channel and surrounding paths perform together. The individual phases remain components of the Porto place account.

sections.heading: Street drainage can use a planted surface
sections.text: The Rua Santos Pousada record dates a rain-garden intervention to 2025. It describes a planted drainage strip receiving runoff from the carriageway and pavement, with infiltration and pretreatment before water reaches the culverted Poço das Patas stream. The feature connects a street-renewal project with the downstream drainage system rather than treating rainfall as only an underground-pipe problem. Its results panel refers to temporary retention and controlled drainage for regulatory events. That is not proof that every extreme storm is contained or that flooding has been eliminated. Continued performance depends on the actual installation, maintenance and conditions across the receiving catchment.

sections.heading: Household energy support is a regional service
sections.text: AdEPorto describes the Energy Hub as integrated support for building efficiency, renewable energy and self-consumption across northern Portugal. Its examples include insulation, glazing, heating and cooling, with citizens and housing-management bodies among the intended users. This connects household comfort with decisions that can be difficult to navigate, including technical options and project implementation. The service’s availability is not itself a completed retrofit, verified household saving or grant guarantee. A useful municipal account would distinguish advice provided, works completed and subsequent conditions in homes, while keeping the regional programme’s reach separate from the number of Porto residents actually served.

sections.heading: Editorial test for water and energy improvements
sections.text: Follow a small set of neighbourhood interventions and service users through clearly defined stages. For drainage, link the installed feature to maintenance, rainfall intensity and conditions downstream. For utility performance, retain the original denominator and distinguish reported annual figures from daily operating data. For household energy, separate an advice encounter from completed work and from sustained comfort or lower consumption. These distinctions allow different services to be compared without pretending that they share one measure of success. The resulting Porto account should explain practical connections between public space, water and homes while exposing the limits of each reported result.

next_artifacts: Underlying utility definitions and comparable annual operating records, including actual non-potable reuse deliveries.
Maintenance and rainfall-event observations for Asprela and Rua Santos Pousada with catchment boundaries.
Anonymized Energy Hub service, completed-retrofit and household-condition evidence separated by municipality and stage.
